index.title: Two Schemes That Store the Same Four Numbers
index.prompt: The running example's 2 heads cost 8 numbers of cache per token, and both multi-query attention and multi-head latent attention bring that down to 4. Compute what head 2 returns for "cat" under each scheme, and say which one changes the head's answer and what each gives up in return. 3 parts.
index.answer: Worked solutions are given part by part on the problem page. Attempt each part on paper before revealing it.

theory.title: Two Schemes That Store the Same Four Numbers
overview: The running example has one layer, 2 heads of 2 numbers, and a token vector of 4 numbers, so a token costs 8 numbers of cache when every head keeps its own keys and values. Two schemes bring that down to 4 numbers per token:

list: **Multi-query attention.** One stored set, head 1's, which both heads read. Head 2 keeps its own queries.
**Multi-head latent attention.** One stored vector per token, the token vector itself, and every head's key and value are computed from it with that head's own weights.

setup.p: The three tokens carry the vectors (1.000, 1.000, 0.000, 1.000) for "the", (0.841, 1.540, 1.010, 1.000) for "cat" and (0.909, −0.416, 1.020, 2.000) for "sat". Head 2's query for "cat" is (1.540, 1.000). Its key of a token is the second and fourth numbers of the token vector and its value the third and fourth. In head 1 the key of a token is the second and third numbers and its value the first and second.

prompt.p: Under multi-head latent attention, what does head 2 return for "cat"? Give the first of its two numbers.

answer.p: The rebuild uses head 2's own weights, so nothing about the head changes: it sees the same query and the same keys and values it would have stored for itself. Its key of "cat" is (1.540, 1.000) and its value is (1.010, 1.000).

Against the three keys of head 2, (1.000, 1.000), (1.540, 1.000) and (−0.416, 2.000), the dot products are 2.540, 3.372 and 1.359, and dividing by 1.414 gives 1.796, 2.384 and 0.961. With the largest subtracted the terms are 0.555, 1.000 and 0.241, which total 1.796, giving weights 0.309, 0.557 and 0.134. The weighted sum of the values is
The first number is 0.699, and it is the head's own answer, unchanged.

prompt.p: Under multi-query attention, what does head 2 return for "cat"? Give the first of its two numbers.

answer.p: Now the keys and values behind head 2 are head 1's. The query is still head 2's own, (1.540, 1.000), and the keys are now (1.000, 0.000), (1.540, 1.010) and (−0.416, 1.020). The dot products are 1.540, 3.382 and 0.379, so the scores are 1.089, 2.391 and 0.268. With the largest subtracted the terms are 0.272, 1.000 and 0.120, which total 1.392, giving weights 0.195, 0.719 and 0.086 when each is worked out before rounding.
The values are head 1's, (1.000, 1.000), (0.841, 1.540) and (0.909, −0.416), so the weighted sum is

The first number is 0.878, up from 0.699. The weights moved from (0.309, 0.557, 0.134) to (0.195, 0.719, 0.086), so part of the change is where the head looks, and the rest is the values it brings back.

prompt.p: Both schemes store 4 numbers per token. One of them changes what head 2 returns and the other does not. Which is which, and what does the comparison say about what each of them has to give up?

answer.p: Multi-query attention changes head 2's answer, from (0.699, 1.134) to (0.878, 1.266), and it changes it for every token in the text. Head 2 still chooses where to look, but the numbers it brings back are head 1's, so a head whose job was to fetch something else now returns something else. Multi-head latent attention leaves every head's answer exactly as it was, since each head rebuilds its own key and value from the shared vector with its own weights.

So the two schemes spend the same 4 numbers per token and buy different things. Multi-query attention saves memory by giving up per-head values. Multi-head latent attention keeps them, so its saving has to come from somewhere else: from one compressed vector per token instead of a stored set for every head. That is what DeepSeek-V2 does, storing 512 numbers of latent and 64 more for the position, 576 in all, against 256 for one shared set of 128, and 576 ÷ 256 = 2.25 shared sets rather than one. A real latent also has to lose something, since it is a compressed copy, and the open question is how much each head can afford to lose.
